#  The education of Christopher Nolan: Why the legendary director avoided studying film in university 
Trending
[Claudia Khaw](https://studyinternational.com/author/claudia-khaw/)
31 Jul 2026 
![Christopher Nolan](https://studyinternational.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ChristopherNolanIMAXCrop-byPhilipRomano-768x537.jpg) Christopher Nolan at the NYC Premiere of "The Odyssey" on July 14, 2026. Source: Philip Romano via Wiki Commons 
[ ![Share on Facebook](https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) ](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) [ ![Share on X](https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) ](https://twitter.com/share?url=https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/&text=The%20education%20of%20Christopher%20Nolan:%20Why%20the%20legendary%20director%20avoided%20studying%20film%20in%20university) [ ![Share on whatsapp](https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) ](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=The%20education%20of%20Christopher%20Nolan:%20Why%20the%20legendary%20director%20avoided%20studying%20film%20in%20university%20https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) Link copied ![Share this article](https://studyinternational.com/news/christopher-nolan-education-university/) Copy link text
Unless you’ve been living under a very large, very soundproof rock, you know “The Odyssey” just dropped. No, not the Homer book, that’s been out for, like, 2,700 years.
Christopher Nolan’s three-hour, R-rated, shot-entirely-on-IMAX-film adaptation of Homer’s 3,000-year-old epic poem hit cinemas on July 17, 2026.
And, clearly, love for the classics is well and alive because it opened to over US$264 million globally in its first weekend alone, making it Nolan’s biggest opening ever. Two weekends in, it had already crossed US$650 million worldwide. Yes, for a nearly three-hour R-rated movie about a guy trying to get home from war.

In 2026. That’s the kind of pull only a handful of directors on the planet have.
Which makes us wonder, what is Christopher Nolan’s own origin story? What we found was pretty wild — including the fact that he studied something that has basically nothing to do with directing, and that his family has a plot twist stranger than anything in his filmography.

## Who is Christopher Nolan?
If you’ve somehow only vibes-known Nolan as “the Batman guy” or “the guy who made time confusing in Tenet,” here’s the quick rundown: Christopher Edward Nolan was born on 30 July 1970 in London, to a British ad copywriter dad and an American teacher mum, which is basically why he holds both UK and US citizenship and has spent his career splitting the difference between British indie sensibility and full-blown Hollywood scale.
He got his hands on a Super-8 camera at age 7 and never really put a camera down again. He started gaining recognition through indie acclaim, starting with his micro-budget debut “Following” (1998).
Fast forward a few decades, and he’s the guy behind a list of blockbusters, including:
  * Memento
  * The Prestige
  * The Dark Knight trilogy
  * Inception
  * Interstellar
  * Dunkirk
  * Tenet
  * Oppenheimer


Can you believe he’s only won his first Best Director Oscar in 2024 for Oppenheimer (which also won Best Picture)? Well, he’s also, as of September 2025, the sitting President of the Directors Guild of America. So yeah. He’s kind of a big deal.

## The surprising education of Christopher Nolan
For someone who loves film so much, it might be surprising to learn that Christopher Nolan did _not_ go to[ film school.](https://studyinternational.com/news/best-film-schools/)
But he studied something maybe just as relevant, if not _more._ He pursued English Literature at University College London (UCL).
It wasn’t that Nolan didn’t try pursuing film. Years after graduating, [Nolan was interviewed](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/what-was-like-teach-christopher-nolan-director-ucl/) by a film professor, Professor Philip Horne. Nolan told him, “Your film class is the only film class I’ve done in my life. It was bloody irritating, actually. No fault of yours. In a good way, it put me off ever studying film in that way, because if you want to be a filmmaker, I couldn’t sit there; it’s much easier to do it with books. With films, I was already too conscious of the compromises you make every day on set.”
With literature, he got to pick up a whole new way of thinking about storytelling: he’s talked about how novelists have had narrative freedom for centuries (flashbacks, unreliable narrators, jumping around in time) that filmmakers had gotten boxed out of once TV made linear storytelling the default.
That idea — steal the freedom novelists always had — basically became his whole directorial thesis. Memento’s reverse chronology, Inception’s nested dream layers, Tenet’s inverted time, Dunkirk’s three overlapping timelines — all of it can be traced back to his literary background.
While he was studying at UCL, though, something that was highly relevant for him was the Union Film Society, where he became president and started shooting 16mm films. He also funded his summer film projects by screening movies during term time.
It was scrappy, self-taught, guerrilla-style filmmaking — the same DIY instincts he used to make his first feature, Following (1998), on a budget of roughly US$6,000, reportedly.
## **Wait, what’s this about an assassin brother?**
_This_ is the part of Nolan lore that goes viral every couple of years and genuinely sounds made up.
Christopher Nolan has two brothers: Jonathan Nolan, who co-wrote Memento, The Prestige, The Dark Knight, Interstellar, and co-created Westworld.
Then, there’s Matthew Nolan, the older brother, who has never worked in film. And this man has an unhinged backstory involving the FBI, Interpol, a fake identity, and an accusation of contract killing.
Here’s the gist: In 2005, an American accountant named Robert Cohen was found dead in Costa Rica after being kidnapped. Investigators eventually connected Matthew Nolan to the case, and it turned out the FBI had actually been watching him since 2005 in connection with a separate bank fraud scheme back in Chicago. While under investigation, he [allegedly](https://www.reddit.com/r/Letterboxd/comments/1v44u6d/nolans_oldest_brother_was_an_alleged_assassin_who/) used the alias “Matthew Oppenheimer.” Yes — _Oppenheimer_.
Some Redditors “joke” that Christopher Nolan made the film to cover his tracks. All alleged, of course. Ahem.
Matthew was arrested in the US, and while he was never actually convicted of murder (someone else was convicted in the Cohen case), he did plead guilty to charges tied to the fraud scheme. While in custody awaiting extradition proceedings, [he was reported](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2010/07/07/nolan-sentenced-for-escape-attempt/) to have attempted to escape federal prison using a 31-foot rope made of bedsheets, a makeshift harness, and tools to pick handcuffs. It didn’t work. He served time and was released around 2010, and neither Christopher nor Jonathan has ever publicly spoken about him since.
Matt Damon, Christopher Nolan, Emma Thomas, and Anne Hathaway at the NYC Premiere of “The Odyssey” on July 14, 2026. Source: Philip Romano via Wiki Commons
## **Should you _not_ study film if you want to be a good director? **
Christopher Nolan’s story is a pretty solid reminder that the “correct” path into directing doesn’t really exist. He’s proof that studying something different — literature, in his case — can end up shaping your creative voice more than a technical degree would.
And actually, there are a couple of other famous directors who chose to study a language instead of film:
  * **Martin Scorsese** earned a bachelor’s degree in English from New York University (NYU) in 1964, though he stayed at NYU to complete his master’s degree in film.
  * **Steven Spielberg** studied English at Cal State Long Beach (and was famously rejected from USC’s film school — twice).
  * **Greta Gerwig** studied English and philosophy at Barnard College before ever picking up directing.


But there are also tons of film directors who pursued lots of different things to start. Dune director Denis Villeneuve studied physics before switching to film production in Quebec. Wong Kar-Wai studied Graphic Design at the Hong Kong Polytechnic before joining a television production training course. The late great Alfred Hitchcock studied engineering and navigation and took night classes in art at the University of London.
A bunch of directors also studied film itself and turned out just fine. Spike Lee earned his Master of Fine Arts in film from New York University (Tisch), George Lucas studied cinematic arts at the University of Southern California (USC), and Chloé Zhao pursued film production at New York University (Tisch).
The fact is that you can start anywhere and still end up being a phenomenal film director. As the great Ratatouille movie (directed by Brad Bird) says, a great cook can come from anywhere.
